title: Waste-Fat Origin Passports for 45Z Fuel
one_liner: Collector-level audits, chain of custody and lab fingerprinting that prove a load of used cooking oil or animal fat is North American.
customer: Renewable diesel, SAF and biodiesel producers, feedstock traders, and UCO collectors who want a price premium for proven origin.
problem: Since 2026, the 45Z clean-fuel credit has been limited to North American feedstocks, which creates an incentive to relabel imported UCO as domestic. Existing testing labs certify samples, not the collection chain, and producers face audit and credit-clawback risk.
solution: An 'origin passport' per load: KYC and site audits of collectors, GPS-tagged pickups, retained samples, and lab fingerprinting (fatty-acid and sterol profile, stable isotopes) against a growing reference library, delivered as per-load certificates and a traceability dashboard.
why_now: The 45Z origin restriction took effect for fuel made after 2025, so proof of origin has become a price factor. A UCO import surge and past fraud scandals mean auditors will look hard.
revenue_model: Per-load certificate fee of a few cents per gallon, annual collector audit fee, and subscription for producers.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is a fraud-prone commodity because the seller controls the paperwork. Verifying the collection chain, not the oil, is where enforcement will go.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 mid-size collectors and one independent biodiesel producer as design partners. Build a reference sample library from those partners. Set up a lab partnership. Run first 20 loads with passports.

title: Live Lyric Captions for Concerts
one_liner: Setlist-conditioned real-time captions of sung lyrics and banter, delivered to phones and smart glasses with translation, sold to venues as an accessibility service.
customer: Venues, festivals and touring promoters with accessibility obligations, plus artists wanting international fans served.
problem: Deaf and hard-of-hearing fans get no lyrics, because speech recognition fails on singing over a loud PA. Human captioning exists for spoken theatre but not concerts, and overseas fans lack translation.
solution: Load the artist's setlist and lyrics ahead of time. Align the sound-desk audio to lyrics with tolerance for improvisation and run speech recognition only on banter. Distribute via a QR-code web page and smart glasses with per-language translation, with a human captioner supervising deviations.
why_now: Display-equipped smart glasses started shipping in late 2025, on-device translation is good enough, and venues face growing accessibility pressure.
revenue_model: $300-1,500 per show for venues plus a paid translation tier from artists' fan clubs, and sponsorship from device makers.
non_obvious_insight: Lyrics are the one thing known in advance, which turns an impossible speech recognition problem into a tractable alignment problem. Accessibility budgets exist but nobody sells a concert-native product.
first_30_days: Test at 3 local shows with two Deaf community groups. Partner with one venue for a free pilot, gather testimonials, and sign 2 venues at $250 per month.

title: Closing-Time Recovery for Shutting Small Businesses
one_liner: A contingency-fee agent that finds and collects the money owners forget when they close: tariff refunds, overpaid taxes, insurance returns, deposits and vendor credits.
customer: Owners of small businesses closing or filing Chapter 7 or Subchapter V (restaurants, boutique importers, e-commerce brands, agencies), plus trustees and wind-down lawyers who will not chase small assets.
problem: Exhausted owners walk away from uncollected money. Customs owes about $166B in IEEPA tariff refunds to roughly 330,000 importers after the Supreme Court struck the tariffs down on February 20, 2026, with refunds running through CBP's CAPE portal and protest windows expiring on a rolling basis. Beyond tariffs, there are overpaid sales and payroll taxes, unearned insurance premium, utility and landlord deposits, vendor credits, customer deposits, workers' comp dividends and unclaimed property. Trustees often skip small claims because the cost outweighs the return.
solution: Run a standard 40-item recovery checklist automatically: pull entry data through a licensed customs-broker partner with a power of attorney, search unclaimed property, send insurer audit and refund requests, and file claims with a partner wind-down attorney. Find leads from PACER filings, state dissolution records, lien releases, landlords and accountants. Take 20-30% of recovered funds and pay nothing if nothing is found.
why_now: Tariff refunds are moving but the deadlines to claim them are rolling off. Higher rates, the energy shock and squeezed lower-income consumers are pushing more small businesses to close. Contingency-fee legal and customs partners are available and CBP now has a digital claim channel.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered amounts, with typical finds of $8-40k per closing business. Referral fees from trustees and lawyers.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest asset in a dying small business is often not equipment but claims against governments and vendors the owner does not know exist. A closing owner has no bandwidth, so willingness to hand over a percentage is high, and the funnel widens in every downturn.
first_30_days: Partner with one wind-down attorney and one customs broker. Pull recent Chapter 7 and Subchapter V filings of importers and closed restaurants and send 300 letters offering no-win-no-fee reviews. Target 10 signed engagements and use the first recoveries as case studies.

title: Play Yards: Phone-Free Adventure Clubs for Tweens
one_liner: Membership 'junk playground' clubs staffed by trained playworkers for ages 9-14 (tools, timber, fire pits, no phones, no lessons), launched first in four-day-school-week districts where Friday is a childcare hole.
customer: Parents of 9-14-year-olds paying $150-250/month for after-school access or $45-60 per full Friday, plus landlords with vacant retail or barns. Some state child-care subsidies and school-choice funds may help later.
problem: Schools are banning phones and governments are restricting youth social media, but kids have nowhere to go for unstructured, semi-supervised time with peers. Structured enrichment (coding camps, leagues) is oversupplied, while true adventure playgrounds are rare, nonprofit and mostly for younger children.
solution: A leased warehouse, church hall or barn plus a yard, stocked with loose parts, real tools and a fire pit, with a 1:12 playworker-to-child ratio. Ship an insurer-approved risk-benefit policy, playworker training, a phone-locker rule and flexible memberships. Anchor demand with full-day Fridays in four-day-week districts, then add weekday afternoons and holiday camps.
why_now: More than 2,100 public schools in 26 states now run four-day weeks and the number is growing, mostly in rural districts with few child-care options. At the same time school phone bans and the 'anxious generation' movement have made parents ask for offline peer time.
revenue_model: Monthly memberships, per-day Friday fees (about $50 x 35-40 Fridays is roughly $2,000 per child per year), birthday parties, holiday camps, and later franchise or license fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not activities, it is unsupervised-feeling time with peers, and what makes it sellable is liability engineering: an insurance-approved risk policy and playwork training that let a for-profit offer what municipalities avoid. Four-day weeks give a ready anchor customer (working parents with an empty Friday) that funds the more interesting weekday model.
first_30_days: Choose a four-day-week district with a supportive superintendent and rent a church hall or barn for about $1k/month. Hire two playworkers, secure a youth-program insurance policy, and pre-sell 25 Friday memberships through school newsletters and Facebook groups. Run four pilot Fridays, gather parent and kid feedback, then add after-school hours.

title: Same-Day Sub and Coach Bench for Home Daycares
one_liner: A membership that guarantees a licensed home daycare a vetted substitute within hours and, when a child's behavior threatens expulsion, an on-call early-childhood coach, so licensed slots stay open and parents keep their jobs.
customer: Licensed family child care providers (solo operators; start with about 300 in one metro or state). Co-payers: state agencies and child-care resource and referral (CCR&R) organizations with workforce-support funds, employers buying backup-care value, and Head Start partners.
problem: Childcare deserts are as much a retention problem as a construction problem. Family homes were the fastest-growing supply (+4.3% in 2024, versus +1.5% for centers), but one sick day closes a solo business, providers work 50-60 hour weeks, and average childcare worker pay is $33,140. Behavior challenges lead to expulsions, and few early-childhood mental health consultants exist to help. Each lost slot means a parent leaves work.
solution: 1) 'Slot Guarantee': a bench of background-checked, trained substitutes (retired teachers, early-education students, displaced parents) dispatched via app on a 2-hour target. 2) 'Calm Team': early-childhood coaches supervised by an infant-mental-health-endorsed clinician, deployed for observation and a behavior plan before expulsion. 3) Monthly Provider Circles of about 8 providers for peer support and reflective supervision. 4) Light back-office (attendance, billing).
why_now: Employer and family demand for childcare is rising with the 45F credit (40-50%) and the $7,500 dependent-care FSA, but supply is thin and fragile. Family homes are the growth segment, so protecting them is the cheapest new capacity. States are already funding workforce supports and early-childhood mental health consultation.
revenue_model: Provider membership of $79-129/mo including a few sub days per quarter, with extra sub hours billed at about $22/hr plus a fee. State or CCR&R contracts per provider. Behavior-coach visits at about $150 each or covered by state mental health consultation funds. Employer backup-care pools.
non_obvious_insight: Every desert plan builds new slots. The cheaper win is stopping existing slots from closing over sick days, burnout and expulsions. The real unit of childcare supply is a provider's mental state, and support for it is a bench of people, not an app.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 providers in one metro through Facebook groups and a CCR&R newsletter with a $59 founding-member rate. Assemble 15 substitutes from retired teachers and early-education students. Partner with one infant-mental-health clinician to lead the first Provider Circles. Approach the local CCR&R or county for a pilot fund, and track closures avoided as the headline metric.

title: Lender-Required Benefit Records for F&I Add-Ons
one_liner: A 20-second, VIN-aware 'did this product actually benefit this buyer' check and signed record that indirect lenders demand as a funding stip, because California's CARS Act (SB 766) bans add-ons that provide no benefit and lenders inherit the exposure.
customer: Primary payer: credit unions and banks that buy indirect auto paper in California (dealer-management and compliance teams). Secondary: California franchised and independent dealer groups, at about $149 per store per month, when a lender tells them to use it.
problem: SB 766 becomes operative Oct 1, 2026. It bars charging for an add-on the buyer would not benefit from, requires clear disclosure that add-ons are optional, and requires dealers to keep records for two years. Lenders that buy the contracts carry Holder Rule and Rees-Levering exposure for what happens in the F&I office. Nobody outside the dealership can see whether GAP was sold to a buyer with 35% down, a 7-year service contract to a buyer with 6 years of factory powertrain warranty left, or prepaid oil changes to an EV buyer. The FTC's federal CARS Rule was vacated in January 2025, so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement, and the April 2026 $78.1M Lindsay Automotive settlement shows the size of the downside.
solution: A lightweight web form and API that the F&I manager fills in per product during the menu. It auto-decodes the VIN (EV or hybrid, remaining factory warranty, tire type, key type). It pulls loan-to-value from the deal numbers and runs benefit rules per product, such as GAP with LTV under about 90%, a service contract that overlaps the factory warranty, maintenance on an EV, and key replacement on a keyless-start car. It flags mismatches, captures a one-tap 'customer chose this anyway, here's why' rationale, and outputs a timestamped PDF and JSON record. Lenders add it to their funding-package checklist. The rule library is the product and is updated per state as CARS-style bills spread.
why_now: SB 766 takes effect in three days (Oct 1, 2026). Federal rule-making is dead, so the compliance burden has moved to states and to lenders' third-party-risk teams. More states are copying California's language. The Lindsay $78.1M settlement in April 2026 made every dealer compliance director and every credit union counsel pay attention.
revenue_model: Per-funded-contract fee of $2 to $4 paid by the lender or passed to the dealer, or a $149 per store per month dealer subscription. Later, sell state-by-state rule packs and an anonymized benefit-mismatch benchmark to lenders and dealer insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Most dealer violations are not lies. They are menu autopilot. The DMS menu shows the same five products on every deal and the pay plan rewards penetration, so a mismatch happens without anyone deciding to deceive. The buyer who will pay for compliance is not the dealer, whose incentive is to sell. It is the lender, who holds the paper, gets sued alongside the dealer, and has the leverage to make a data field mandatory at funding.
first_30_days: Read the SB 766 text and the FTC's vacated rule for the exact 'no benefit' examples, and turn them into 25 to 30 explicit rules. Build a plain web form with no DMS integration. Cold-pitch compliance officers at 15 California credit unions with big indirect books through the CUNA/California credit union compliance channels. Offer a free 60-day pilot in which they require it from their 3 to 5 highest-volume dealers. Pre-sell 10 dealers at $99 per month using the line 'your lender is going to ask for this.'

title: 72-Hour Diligence Engine for Vet Clinic Acquirers
one_liner: Upload a PIMS export and P&L and get retention cohorts, price-versus-volume decomposition and doctor-dependence risk in three days, then keep the same schema as the post-close KPI dashboard.
customer: Mid-size vet groups, search-fund and PE platforms buying 5-50 clinics a year, and practice lenders.
problem: Roll-ups are continuing (GoodVets buying WellHaven, 40+ hospitals), but small acquirers rely on broker packages and QuickBooks. PIMS exports differ by system, and price increases can hide falling active-client counts, a real risk given visits reportedly down three years.
solution: Ingest PIMS exports across major systems, normalize service lines, then compute cohort retention, active clients, revenue per DVM and tech utilization, price/mix/volume decomposition, discount and controlled-substance anomalies, and revenue at risk if the owner-vet leaves. Output a quality-of-earnings-lite memo, then continue as a post-merger KPI dashboard.
why_now: M&A pace is high, buyers include newer and smaller platforms without in-house analytics, and LLMs make messy export mapping cheap. Incumbents such as IDEXX are buying workflow AI (CoVet), not diligence tooling.
revenue_model: $3-6K per target for diligence, $1-2K per clinic per month for post-close dashboards.
non_obvious_insight: The price hikes that flatter EBITDA may be masking client attrition. Diligence that sees through price versus volume is worth far more than its fee, and brokers will not build it because it works against their headline numbers.
first_30_days: Approach 10 mid-size groups and search funds with a free retrospective on one closed deal. Build export mappers for 3 major PIMS. Sell 3 paid diligences at $3K each.

title: Section 8 Rent-Increase Deadline Capture Service
one_liner: A tracker that knows each voucher tenant's lease anniversary, sees the new FY2027 payment standard, and files the landlord's rent-increase request inside the tight 60-day window before a year of raise is forfeited.
customer: Small landlords with 1 to 50 Housing Choice Voucher units, especially out-of-state investors in Section 8-heavy markets such as Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis and Indianapolis. Small PM firms with voucher portfolios are the second segment.
problem: Housing-authority payment standards rose for FY2027, but a new standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1. It applies only at each tenant's lease anniversary. The owner must send a written request within a typically tight window, often 60 days before that date, or forfeit the increase for a year. Each housing authority has its own forms and dates. Most small owners never map the anniversary dates, so they leave real money uncollected. One market analysis found 3-bedroom increases of 6 to 12%, with a median of 10%.
solution: The landlord uploads photos of their HAP contracts and leases, and the tool extracts tenant anniversary dates and current contract rents. The team maintains a database of housing-authority payment standards and each authority's request process (scraped from PHA PDFs and notices, human-verified). For each unit it computes the increase headroom, alerts at 90, 75 and 60 days before the window closes, and generates the authority-specific rent-increase request letter or form. It tracks proof of submission and logs who was contacted and when. It also flags likely mistakes in the original rent-reasonableness record (wrong bedroom count or square footage) that justify a correction request mid-lease.
why_now: FY2027 standards take effect around October 1, 2026, and today is 2026-09-28. Anniversary windows are opening across the country right now. The forum thread on this appeared within days, and the one-year forfeiture is a hard deadline that makes people spend money.
revenue_model: Success-aligned pricing: $5 per unit per month, plus 1 month of the captured increase for each unit where the request is approved. On a $1,300 rent and a 10% bump, that is $130 per month, or $1,560 a year, per unit. Authority data is the moat; a PM-firm plan can charge per door. Later, a similar deadline tracker can cover annual recertification and inspection dates.
non_obvious_insight: The money is lost to a calendar, not to the tenant or the market, and the people who feel it are the least likely to be organized. A BiggerPockets post titled 'Section 8 rents went up for FY2027. Most landlords won't collect it' says: 'A new payment standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1'. It adds that owners must submit written requests within a typically tight 60-day window before each anniversary or forfeit the opportunity for an entire year. It reports 3-bedroom rates up 6-12% (median 10%) in nine of ten low-cost ZIP codes, and notes that St. Louis adopted its FY2027 standards effective Jan 1, 2027 (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1301792-section-8-rents-went-up-for-fy2027-most-landlords-wont-collect-it). Out-of-state voucher landlords also struggle with local rules, as in a Cleveland thread on Section 8 inspection standards (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302305-furnace-and-water-heater-on-wood-platforms-cleveland-section-8-inspection). A separate thread notes Section 8 tenants are 'already at maximum allowable rates' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302138-how-realistic-is-it-to-raise-rents-100-on-existing-tenants).
first_30_days: Week 1: hand-build payment-standard tables and request procedures for 3 housing authorities (start with St. Louis, Cleveland and Memphis). Publish a free calculator, 'How much did you leave on the table this year?', in the BiggerPockets Out-of-State and Landlording forums. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 15 landlords, send requests manually with the templates, and track approvals. Week 4: turn on success-fee billing, and pitch 3 small voucher-heavy PM firms. Target: 15 landlords, 100+ units, and 10 documented approved increases.

title: Part-Time Seats: Districts Sell Classes to Homeschoolers
one_liner: Software and a playbook that lets shrinking districts enroll homeschoolers and microschoolers a la carte and capture per-pupil funding they are now losing.
customer: Declining-enrollment suburban and rural districts and small charters (superintendents, budget directors) in states that allow part-time or shared-time enrollment.
problem: K-12 enrollment fell from 50.8M to 49.4M (2019-24) and is projected at 46.9M by 2031, with more than 1,000 closures in 2025-26. Districts treat homeschool and microschool families as lost. Yet only about 10% of homeschool families do it K-12 exclusively and 30% do it for 1-2 years (lower-confidence data), so many want labs, band, AP, CTE shops and sports.
solution: A part-time enrollment desk: a catalog of under-filled classes (chem lab, band, welding shop, AP), a family portal for enrollment, records, immunization and attendance, FTE and funding counting per state rules, a la carte billing, and transcript conversion for re-entry. The pitch is that a marginal seat in an empty class costs nearly nothing.
why_now: The enrollment cliff has become a budget crisis. Homeschool ESA families are second-class (Texas homeschoolers get $2,000 against $10,474 for private-school kids), and over 70% of homeschoolers in non-ESA states say they would take public funds. Scholarship-credit and ESA dollars from 2027 can pay for a la carte seats.
revenue_model: $8-25k per year SaaS per district, or a per-enrollment fee of $50-150, or a 5-10% share of incremental revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Districts fight choice by trying to keep full-time kids, but the untapped resource is empty seats in existing classes. Transient and hybrid families are exactly the buyers, and part-time enrollment doubles as a re-entry ramp that brings kids back.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a clear part-time or shared-time statute. Recruit 2 budget-stressed districts for a free pilot. Publish the seat catalog to local homeschool groups. Measure seats sold for the January semester and funding captured.

title: Caring Contacts as a Service for Hospitals
one_liner: Outsourced, human-edited follow-up messages and calls after a suicide-risk emergency visit or crisis call, run on a compliance-grade platform hospitals and 988 centers can buy per patient.
customer: Hospital EDs and behavioral units, state-funded 988 crisis centers, university counseling centers and behavioral-health carve-out plans, paying $40-120 per patient enrolled or $5-15k a month per site.
problem: The highest-risk window is the weeks after discharge or a crisis call. The Joint Commission's NPSG 15.01.01 requires follow-up policy, and randomized trials of brief, non-demanding 'caring contact' messages show fewer attempts. Yet most systems run this through one overwhelmed staffer mailing postcards, with no delivery guarantee, tracking or outcome reporting.
solution: A managed service: enrollment at discharge on a tablet, a cadence built from an evidence-based message library (days 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 and beyond), AI drafting with human review, two-way replies routed to trained staff, escalation with warm handoff to crisis lines, and EHR-connected dashboards for Joint Commission and Zero Suicide reporting.
why_now: 988 volume has grown since 2022, about a dozen states now levy 988 telecom fees that fund local centers, and the Harvard study estimating 4,400 fewer youth and young-adult suicide deaths in 988's first 2.5 years strengthens the funding case. 988 politics (Press 3 ended Jul 2025, a restored version excluding Trevor Project announced Jun 2026) push centers toward reliable, defensible operations.
revenue_model: Per-enrollee fee plus platform fee, funded by hospital quality budgets, state 988 funds and SAMHSA grants.
non_obvious_insight: The market chases AI that detects risk, but the best-evidenced and cheapest intervention is a human-sent, non-demanding note. The product is operations and proof (reliable delivery, documentation, outcome reporting), not detection.
first_30_days: Partner with one county crisis center and one hospital ED. Write the message library with a clinical advisor who knows the caring-contacts literature. Enroll 100 patients on a $10k pilot and measure re-contact and re-presentation rates.

title: Security Grant Desk for Small Congregations
one_liner: Flat-fee application, vulnerability-assessment and post-award compliance packages for small houses of worship using FEMA's Nonprofit Security Grant Program and state equivalents.
customer: Small synagogues, mosques, churches, gurdwaras and temples, and umbrella bodies such as federations, dioceses and mosque councils.
problem: FY2026 NSGP offered $300M (notice published 24 June 2026, deadline extended to 24 July) at up to $200k per site. Applications need a vulnerability assessment, an investment justification and SAM.gov and UEI registration. Small congregations lack the administrative capacity, and post-award procurement and reimbursement rules trip them.
solution: Templated assessments built on CISA's free self-assessment, an investment-justification drafting workflow with security-vendor quote gathering, SAM and UEI onboarding, a state-agency deadline tracker, and post-award procurement and reimbursement compliance. Flat fees only, because FEMA guidance generally bars contingent-fee grant writing.
why_now: FY2026 awards are being announced now and FY2027 prep starts this fall. Threat levels keep congregations motivated.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per application, $800 for post-award compliance, and $150/month trackers for federations.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier is administrative capacity, not eligibility, and referrals flow through community federations. Post-award compliance is the neglected second revenue stream.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 regional federations or mosque councils, run free FY2027-prep webinars, and sell 10 assessment packages. Build a network of vetted security installers for quotes.

title: Findings Sentinel: A Nurse Tracks Your Scan Follow-Ups
one_liner: What a concierge doctor really sells is closed loops: someone reads every report and owns the follow-up; for $20/mo, a nurse-in-the-loop sentinel makes sure your incidental scan findings do not fall through the cracks.
customer: Adults 50-80 (and their adult children) who had a CT, MRI, ultrasound or pathology in the last three years. Incidentals include lung nodules, thyroid, adrenal and kidney lesions, pancreatic cysts and aneurysms. Secondary buyers are self-insured employers, Medicare Advantage plans and imaging centers that carry follow-up liability.
problem: Studies of incidental findings report follow-up failure rates commonly in the 30-60% range (lung nodules especially). The ordering physician is often not notified beyond the report, the PCP is not copied, and under the Cures Act patients see results in portals before anyone explains them. A concierge doctor reads everything and calls; everyone else gets an unread PDF.
solution: Pull records through patient-directed access (Medicare App Library apps, Apple Health Records, portals) or PDF upload. An LLM extracts each 'recommend follow-up in X months' statement and tracks whether it happened. An RN or NP reviews flagged items and issues a plain-language one-pager with the question to ask and a drafted message or referral request to the PCP. A monthly digest and annual records reconciliation are included. No diagnosis or prescribing, so it is navigation, not telemedicine.
why_now: CMS's Health Tech Ecosystem launched its Medicare App Library in April 2026 with hundreds of organizations pledged to FHIR-based sharing, and TEFCA-style patient access is maturing. LLMs are reliable at extracting follow-up recommendations from radiology text, the same technique hospital nodule programs use. That makes nurse minutes rare and targeted.
revenue_model: $20/mo membership; $99 one-time 'catch-up review' of the last three years; $2-4 per member per month from employers and Medicare Advantage plans; imaging centers pay for closed-loop follow-up as risk reduction. Rough cost basis: extraction costs pennies and, if about 8% of members are flagged yearly at about 25 nurse minutes, clinical labor is only a few dollars per member per year.
non_obvious_insight: The concierge doctor's value is not the 60-minute visit; it is that a competent person reads every report and owns the loop. Loop closure is an insurance-like utilization problem: about 95% of members have nothing to flag most months, so the pooled cost fits $20/mo. Immediate-release results created a new market for 'someone to tell me what this means and what happens next'.
first_30_days: Manually pilot with 30 volunteers recruited from incidentaloma communities and senior centers. Members upload reports, a contract RN reviews them, and you count unclosed loops. Publish the results ('X% had an unclosed loop') for PR, and use them to sign one imaging center or employer pilot before building the app.

title: Member-Owned Healthspan Co-ops on the HSA Cap
one_liner: Affinity groups of 300-400 households co-own a small primary-care practice on a roughly $99-129 monthly membership that is now HSA-compatible, use group visits, and buy elite screening at pooled cash prices.
customer: Self-employed and small-business households aged 40-64 on bronze, catastrophic or high-deductible plans who already belong to a trusted group: a congregation, a 55+ community, a chamber of commerce or freelancers' guild, a farmers-market vendors' association, a large local gym.
problem: Elite prevention is sold item by item at retail prices ($200-$2,500 per test), by clinics whose upsell incentives people distrust. Direct primary care exists but rarely includes a preventive protocol and does not pool purchasing power. High deductibles leave the middle class with either a rushed annual physical or nothing between that and an emergency.
solution: A consumer co-op that hires one physician, one NP or health coach and part-time admin on a fixed monthly fee under the direct-primary-care rules. Monthly group visits (60-90 minutes, about 12 members each) cover a rotating theme (blood pressure, lipids and ApoB, sleep, strength, metabolic health) with each member's numbers on a private dashboard, plus 1:1 visits, messaging and same-week appointments. The co-op negotiates cash prices for in-office and send-out labs, coronary calcium scans, DEXA and VO2 testing (paid separately as ordinary HSA-eligible medical expenses), and members vote on which tests the protocol includes, so there is no upsell incentive. The startup provides the co-op in a box: legal templates, protocol, software, physician recruiting and a shared purchasing agreement.
why_now: Since January 1, 2026, direct primary care fees of up to $150 per month for an individual ($300 for a family) no longer disqualify someone from an HSA, and bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans became HSA-eligible, opening HSAs to roughly 7.3 million more Americans. That creates a tax-advantaged price point for exactly this product. DPC statutes exist in most states, and cash-price transparency for imaging and labs is improving.
revenue_model: Members pay the co-op $99-129 per month; the startup earns a platform and management fee of about 12-15% (roughly $15-20 per member per month) plus a $10-15k organizing fee per launch. Group purchasing agreements are structured as flat fees to stay clear of anti-kickback problems.
non_obvious_insight: The HSA rule sets a $150 ceiling that is roughly enough to fund a physician and coach if 400 households pool their membership, and the cooperative form solves the two things that block middle-class longevity medicine: trust (members own the practice and vote on the protocol) and price (pooled buying power). Group visits will not improve outcomes by themselves, as the evidence shows they are roughly equivalent to usual care, but they stretch physician time across more patients. Affinity groups already hold the trust and distribution; one founding meeting is the sales cycle.
first_30_days: Pair a burned-out primary-care physician or existing DPC doctor with one affinity group (a 400-member gym or 55+ community works). Hold a 60-minute founding meeting and collect pledge cards for 150 founding members at $99 per month. Get a state-specific legal and HSA-compliance memo on DPC and cooperative structure. Line up wholesale lab accounts and cash-price quotes from two imaging centers. Open in shared space with the first cohort within about 3-4 months.

title: Two-Way Kasuhara Desk for Tiny Japanese Businesses
one_liner: A QR-and-LINE 'complaint lane' plus staff backup button that gives micro-businesses the customer-harassment policy, consultation channel and evidence log Japan now requires.
customer: Owners of Japanese businesses with 1-100 employees that face customers in person (izakaya, clinics, salons, cram schools, taxi and care operators, retail). They pay ¥2,980-9,800 per site per month. Resale channels are sharoushi (labor and social-insurance consultants) and SME insurance agents.
problem: From 1 Oct 2026 every Japanese employer with at least one employee must publish a policy against customer harassment ('kasuhara'), set up and publicize a consultation channel, and have response procedures. There is no phase-in. Most tiny firms have no HR function, no policy and no channel. Staff also hesitate to report incidents. Customers, for their part, now hesitate to voice legitimate complaints.
solution: (1) A QR code at the counter, on receipts and on LINE opens a structured, polite complaint form (what happened, photo, desired resolution). The owner gets a timestamped record, and abusive or threatening messages are flagged. (2) A 'need backup' button in LINE gives frontline staff an anonymous route to a partner sharoushi or counselor. That route is the required consultation channel. (3) A one-tap incident log that creates a dated evidence pack (notes, optional call-recording notice, response taken). (4) A policy, poster and work-rule addendum generator that meets the MHLW guideline. (5) A monthly 'compliance proof' PDF for the day the labor bureau asks.
why_now: The MHLW guideline was published on 26 Feb 2026 and the duty takes effect 1 Oct 2026, three days from today. Incumbent tooling targets call centers, such as SoftBank's SoftVoice AI voice-softener launched Feb 2026. Nothing is priced or packaged for a 5-person restaurant. The Oct 1 news cycle will also push owners to search for a fix.
revenue_model: ¥2,980/month per site (¥9,800 for 10+ staff), ¥30,000 optional setup for work-rule revision, and a 30% recurring rev-share to sharoushi and insurance agents who resell it. A later upsell is per-incident counselor escalation. Insurers may white-label it into SME liability packages.
non_obvious_insight: The law has a hidden chilling effect on the customer side. In the Channel Corporation survey (497 customer-facing employees plus 514 consumers, June 2026), 52.3% of consumers who hit a store error 'let it pass' for fear of being labelled a harasser, and 65.2% wanted AI-mediated ways to raise issues. A product that gives customers a legitimate complaint lane defuses harassment at the source and doubles as the mandatory paper trail. Enforcement is guidance and then naming rather than fines, so buyers want the cheapest defensible record, not AI detection. Only under 10% of firms use technical measures. Evidence: KiteRa survey of 965 workers on 10-11 Sep 2026 found 61.3% with no policy, 68.3% with no publicized channel, 58.6% of firms with 100 or fewer employees with no channel at all, and 19.8% of workers harassed in the past year, of whom 74.9% hesitated to report (https://prtimes.jp/main/html/rd/p/000000130.000045846.html). Channel Corp found 51.7% with no measures at all (https://ecnomikata.com/ecnews/customerservice/51126/). Legal scope and enforcement: https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2026/singapore/customer-harassment-prevention-now-a-statutory-obligation-for-employers-in-japan. Incumbent focus on call centers: https://www.softbank.jp/en/sbnews/entry/20260219_01.
first_30_days: Days 1-3: Ship a free policy-and-poster generator plus a LINE Official Account to catch Oct 1 search traffic, and a landing page in Japanese. Days 4-14: Recruit 5-10 sharoushi (offer 30% recurring share and a white-label report) and 2 local shokokai chambers; sell 'compliance by Friday' to their existing clients. Build the QR complaint form with LINE Messaging API (no app needed) and manually route staff-backup messages to one partner counselor. Days 15-30: Sign 30-50 shops at ¥2,980 and collect 3 named case studies. Ask an SME insurance agency to pilot a bundled offer.

title: DIC Finder for Veteran Families at Funerals
one_liner: A tool that reads a veteran's death certificate, hospice diagnosis and DD-214 to spot survivor benefits the widow does not know exist, sold to funeral homes and hospices rather than to families.
customer: Funeral homes (roughly 18,000 to 19,000 in the U.S.) that want a differentiated service for veteran families, and hospices with veteran programs. State veteran departments and accredited service officers are downstream partners.
problem: The Vietnam-era generation is now in the last phase of life and forms a large share of veteran deaths. The PACT Act (2022) expanded presumptive conditions for Agent Orange, burn pit and other exposures, so many widows may qualify for Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC, on the order of $1,700 a month, check the current rate). Others may qualify for the Aid and Attendance survivor pension, or accrued benefits. Most never file. The death certificate says 'cardiac arrest' or 'respiratory failure' rather than the underlying service-connected condition. The funeral director's VA paperwork is only for the flag, headstone and burial allowance, and nobody reads the chart for exposure history. The hospice chaplain hears the veteran's service story at the bedside and the widow's money worries at the kitchen table, but has no tool to connect them.
solution: A web and mobile intake tool run at the arrangement conference or at the hospice bereavement visit. It photographs the DD-214, asks a 5-minute exposure and service history (deployment dates and locations, unit, conditions), and matches them against presumptive-condition and location lists. It flags likely DIC, survivor pension and accrued-benefit eligibility, and pre-fills VA Form 21P-534EZ. It then hands the case, with a warm introduction, to an accredited VSO representative or an accredited claims agent. The tool also stores the veteran's story fields so a funeral home can honor the person accurately.
why_now: The PACT Act has created a large wave of newly presumptive conditions, and claim volumes at the VA are at record levels. Vietnam-era veterans are aging into their peak mortality years. As I understand VA rules, accredited representatives can only charge fees after an initial decision, and legislation to tighten fees on predatory claim sharks has been moving. That pushes the sustainable model toward a B2B payer, not families. AI document extraction now makes DD-214 and death-certificate parsing cheap and reliable. Confirm current DIC rates and fee rules before launch.
revenue_model: SaaS for funeral homes at $149 to $299 a month per location, with a per-case add-on for premium processing. Hospices and state veteran departments pay a per-completed-referral fee or a flat annual license. The VSO or accredited-agent partner pays for qualified leads only where the rules allow it, so this must be reviewed by counsel. Families pay nothing.
non_obvious_insight: The money is unclaimed not because widows are lazy but because the trigger event is the funeral, and the only professional in the room (the funeral director) has no financial incentive or training to read a service history. Funeral homes will pay to look like heroes to veteran families, since it feeds pre-need referrals for the next generation, which is where their margin lives.
first_30_days: Partner with one accredited county veteran service officer and two independent funeral homes near a large veteran population. Build the intake as a form plus a manual review by the VSO in week one, before any automation. Run 15 real cases at no charge and record dollars unlocked per family. Use those numbers to close five paying funeral homes at $149 a month. Have a veterans-law attorney review the fee and referral structure before charging anyone.

title: Remote Operator-of-Record for Small Water Systems
one_liner: A roll-up of certified operator licenses and contracts, with cheap remote telemetry so one operator can be operator-of-record for 10-30 small systems.
customer: Small towns, rural water districts, mobile-home and RV parks, HOAs and private systems in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Oklahoma and Iowa. The system pays a monthly fee, and state technical-assistance funds can help.
problem: State law requires a certified operator in responsible charge, yet operators are retiring and small systems cannot hire. Missed sampling and reporting cause violations. The 2027 PFAS initial monitoring and the LCRI lead changes (action level tightens Nov 1, 2027) add workload that these systems cannot absorb.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired operators as a paid bench. Install cellular SCADA gateways ($1-3k hardware) and a compliance calendar (sampling, consumer confidence reports, PFAS and lead tasks). Add on-call field technicians. Start with states that allow remote responsible charge, and with private systems where the sales cycle is shortest.
why_now: The retirement wave, the 2027 monitoring and lead deadlines, $7.2B in FY2026 revolving-fund money (some for small-system assistance), and cheap remote telemetry all coincide.
revenue_model: $3-12k/month per system, plus a compliance-concierge upsell for PFAS and lead sampling packages.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation requires a licensed human, not a plant, so the scarce asset is license-hours. Remote monitoring multiplies each license roughly tenfold. The roll-up is of licenses and contracts, not of plants.
first_30_days: Recruit three retired Grade 2-4 operators. Sign five private systems (mobile-home park owners first). Partner with a state rural water association for referrals. Confirm your state's rules on remote responsible charge with the regulator before selling.

title: Outpatient Parvo Kits for Shelters and Low-Cost Clinics
one_liner: Parvo is treated as inpatient-only, but a standardized ambulatory protocol in a box plus remote nurse monitoring can cut cost per case dramatically for shelters that otherwise euthanize.
customer: Municipal animal services, shelters and spay-neuter/low-cost clinics. Secondary: urgent-care clinics serving low-income clients.
problem: Inpatient parvo care often costs thousands of dollars, so shelters and owners choose euthanasia, and vets suffer moral distress. The briefing notes vet care is nearly half of pet-cost inflation since 2019 and that clinicians routinely alter plans for money. The outpatient protocols exist (Colorado State published one in 2017 reporting survival in the range of hospitalization; re-verify in the pilot) but only as PDFs, not as a product with logistics.
solution: A vet-signed kit per case (SC fluids, maropitant, antibiotics, syringes, nutrition support, dosing cards, video training) sold by a partner clinic-of-record. Twice-daily photo/video/weight/hydration logs are reviewed by an RVT desk with DVM sign-off, with hard escalation rules to inpatient transfer. A shared outcome registry proves results to funders. Extend to other ambulatory-able acute problems (uncomplicated gastroenteritis, SC-fluid CKD cats).
why_now: Access philanthropy just scaled (Duffield 2026-09-17; PetSmart Charities), and funders want cost-per-outcome evidence. Shelters are overcrowded and Texas transports have been slowed by screwworm restrictions. Remote VCPR rules are loosening piecemeal, and spectrum-of-care thinking is now mainstream.
revenue_model: $150-300 per case for kit plus monitoring, versus thousands for inpatient care. Annual shelter subscription ($2-5K) with usage tiers, often paid from grant dollars. Protocol licensing to low-cost clinic chains.
non_obvious_insight: The 'standard of care' for parvo is partly a business-model artifact: hospitals are paid to hospitalize. Nobody sells the cheaper protocol as a logistics-and-monitoring product, and the buyers (shelters, funders) are motivated by lives saved per dollar.
first_30_days: Partner with 3 shelters and one shelter-medicine vet. Assemble kits from wholesale distributors via the vet's prescriptions. Run 20 cases with structured data on survival, days to eating and cost. Apply for a $10K micro-grant to underwrite the pilot. Publish a one-page outcomes summary.

title: Grid-Code Commissioning for AI Campuses
one_liner: A test-and-certify service that validates how an AI campus behaves toward the grid (ride-through, load swings, oscillations), produces the field data transmission owners now must demand, and signs off on it.
customer: Owners of 50-500 MW computational-load sites (neoclouds, colo developers, hyperscalers' second-tier builds) that must satisfy a transmission owner's new commissioning process. Secondary: commissioning agents lacking grid-side capability who subcontract the work, and utilities that want a standard test-and-model package to accept.
problem: Traditional commissioning tests the facility against its own failures: pull the utility feed, gensets pick up, resistive load banks hold steady load. It does not test how UPS systems, rectifiers and GPU power supplies respond to voltage sags and frequency dips, or how synchronized training-job power swings interact with the grid. In July 2024 about 1,500 MW of data center load in Virginia dropped off in seconds. NERC's May 2026 Level 3 alert now calls for detailed load modeling, annual stability studies and a commissioning process for computational loads. Transmission owners have nothing to point at, owners have no test protocol, and everyone is using generic vendor models.
solution: A hardware-agnostic test package. Rent existing programmable AI-load emulators (Vertiv, PowerLoad and other liquid-cooled GPU-emulating load banks already exist), add high-speed PMU and power-quality recorders, and run a standard protocol: voltage and frequency ride-through, ramp and step-load profiles from real training traces, oscillation checks, and backup-transfer behavior under dynamic load. Deliver a PE-stamped report and an EMT/PSS/E model-validation dataset shaped for the transmission owner's interconnection group. Offer the same protocol to utilities as a certificate template. The value is the protocol, the sign-off and the model validation, not the hardware.
why_now: NERC issued a Level 3 Alert on May 4, 2026. FERC ordered NERC to file mandatory reliability standards for computational loads by Dec 31, 2026. Texas's SB 6 large-load rule is also expected by year end. The emulator hardware finally exists, but the commissioning process and accepted evidence package do not. The first owners to energize in late 2026 and 2027 will need this or wait months for the utility to sign off.
revenue_model: $150K-400K fixed fee per site (test campaign, report, model validation). $30K-80K per additional hall. Subcontract margin when working under Cx agents. Annual re-test and monitoring subscription of $40K-100K per site. Later, licensing of the protocol to utilities.
non_obvious_insight: Commissioning teams are excellent at proving the facility survives a grid failure and almost blind to proving the grid survives the facility. The IST script stops at the fence line. The utility's planners are working from datasheet models that nobody has ever field-validated, and the person best placed to bridge the two (a data center Cx lead who has run a hundred pull-the-plug tests) has never talked to a transmission planner.
first_30_days: Hire or partner with 2 power-systems engineers (an EMT/protection specialist and a load-bank/field-test lead). Write a public 'reading the NERC Level 3 alert as a commissioning test plan' whitepaper. Pitch 5 commissioning agents on white-label subcontract. Line up an emulator rental partner. Offer a discounted pilot to a 20-50 MW neocloud or colo site heading for energization in the next 6 months, priced at cost in exchange for a published (anonymized) case study and a transmission owner introduction.

title: Fixed-Price MDR Clinical Evaluation Reports via ASReview
one_liner: A tech-enabled service that uses the open-source ASReview active-learning screener plus medical writers to deliver audit-ready literature-based Clinical Evaluation Reports at a fraction of consultant prices.
customer: EU MDR device makers with 5-50 staff: digital-health and software-as-a-medical-device startups, legacy Class I/IIa/IIb device makers, and regulatory consultants who need white-label capacity.
problem: MDR requires a Clinical Evaluation Report built on a systematic literature review with appraisal, state-of-the-art analysis and ongoing updates. Consultants charge roughly EUR 10-40k for a literature-based CER. Small firms delay certification or withdraw legacy products because of clinical-evaluation cost.
solution: Run the search protocol in PubMed and other open sources, ClinicalTrials.gov and vigilance databases. Screen with ASReview LAB (validated in Nature Machine Intelligence) with the full screening log retained. A medical writer and a clinical expert appraise and sign off. Deliver the CER plus a PRISMA-style flow diagram and search-string appendix, then sell a quarterly 'living' update for post-market clinical follow-up.
why_now: Legacy-device MDR transition deadlines fall in 2027-2028 and notified-body capacity is tight. Half of medtechs report expecting to spend 5% or more of revenue on MDR. ASReview is mature and widely used in academia, but no one packages it for regulatory work.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of EUR 4-9k per literature-based CER on low-risk devices. Recurring literature-update subscriptions of EUR 1.2-3k per year. Wholesale white-label pricing for consultancies.
non_obvious_insight: Notified bodies rarely reject a CER because the science is thin. They reject it because the methodology is undocumented: search protocol, appraisal criteria, equivalence reasoning. ASReview's transparent, reproducible logging is the compliance artifact, so sell reproducibility rather than speed.
first_30_days: Recruit two freelance medical writers and one clinician-reviewer. Publish three sample CER sections for a public device category as proof. Post in regulatory-affairs communities (RAPS chapters, MDR LinkedIn groups). Sell the first five CERs at a design-partner price and use the audit trail from each as the case study.

title: Robot Finger That Makes Legacy Instruments Agent-Operable
one_liner: A camera-plus-servo retrofit box that presses buttons, turns knobs and reads displays on validated lab and test equipment from the outside, giving decade-old instruments an API without touching their software.
customer: QC and analytical labs in pharma and CDMOs, food and environmental testing labs, university core facilities, and small biotechs running out-of-support equipment such as plate readers, autoclaves, centrifuges, HPLC pumps, stability chambers and test benches.
problem: Lab automation assumes new, API-enabled instruments, but the installed base is 10-20-year-old boxes with front panels only. In GxP and ISO 17025 labs, changing instrument firmware or software can trigger revalidation, which blocks IT-style integration. Scientists and agents still want unattended overnight runs, scheduling and structured logs.
solution: A clamp-on or adhesive module with 2-6 servos for buttons, knobs and a touchscreen stylus, a wide-angle camera, and a vision-language model that reads 7-segment displays, LCDs and status LEDs. A confirm-after-every-action loop and hard interlocks make it safe. It exposes an MCP and REST endpoint ('start program 4', 'read temperature', 'log state') and keeps video plus state log as the audit trail. It sits outside the validated boundary as 'operator-equivalent', so only the actuator needs qualification.
why_now: Vision-language models now read messy panels cheaply and reliably, and servo and edge-compute costs are trivial. Autonomous-lab offerings such as Ginkgo Cloud Lab prove scientists want agent-run experiments, but they require shipping samples to a vendor's lab. Most labs still own and must keep using their own equipment.
revenue_model: $400-900 hardware per instrument, $40-100 per month per device for scheduling, audit trail and the agent endpoint, and $2-5k per site for IQ/OQ qualification templates.
non_obvious_insight: Revalidation cost, not technology, blocks lab automation. An actuator that does exactly what a technician's finger does sidesteps change control, so selling 'validation-friendly' beats selling 'smart'. The video-verified state log is also a better audit trail than most instruments produce natively.
first_30_days: Build 3 prototypes from off-the-shelf servos, cameras and a Raspberry Pi-class board. Interview 20 QC lab managers and core-facility directors. Offer free two-week pilots on one autoclave or plate reader that runs a nightly routine, then convert to a $3k paid pilot including an IQ/OQ document.

title: Aid-in-Dying Program-in-a-Box for Hospices
one_liner: Sell newly-legal states' hospices and health systems the policies, forms, trained consulting-clinician panel and logistics they need to participate in medical aid in dying.
customer: Independent hospices, palliative practices and non-religious health systems in Illinois and New York, then Massachusetts and Pennsylvania if they pass. The buyer is the medical director or administrator.
problem: Legalization creates a right on paper. The bottleneck is willing, trained clinicians (attending plus consulting physician, and mental-health evaluation where required), statutory documentation, waiting periods, pharmacy sourcing and staff opt-out policies. Most providers have no playbook, so patients bounce between systems that opt out. Advocacy groups cover navigation, not staffing.
solution: A turnkey program: policy templates, staff training, state-specific e-documentation workflows, an on-call roster of trained consulting physicians and evaluators (licensed per state, telehealth where allowed), pharmacy coordination, family support, and post-death reporting. The service serves only patient-initiated requests and supports providers that opt in.
why_now: New York's law was signed Feb 6, 2026, and Illinois's law, signed Dec 12, 2025, takes effect this month (Sept 2026). Two large states are opening within months, with 14 jurisdictions now having some form of law and more pending. Scheduled deaths also create planning lead time that sudden deaths never had.
revenue_model: $15-40K program onboarding fee, $500-$1,000 per consult or evaluation, and per-case coordination fees. State grants are possible.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not legal permission but willing clinicians and paperwork bandwidth, so the money is in clinical capacity and compliance, which advocacy nonprofits don't provide.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 physicians with prior Oregon or Washington experience as advisors. Approach 10 independent Illinois hospices. Sell a $7.5K readiness assessment plus policy pack first. Start recruiting a consulting-physician roster and get counsel to confirm state rules on telehealth and referral fees.

title: Second-Life Studio: Shelved Human Drugs for Dogs
one_liner: Mine the wreckage of failed human biotechs for safe, clinical-stage molecules that make viable dog and cat drugs, and broker them to animal-health companies.
customer: Animal-health business-development teams (Zoetis, Elanco, Dechra, Boehringer AH, Merck AH, Ceva, Virbac) and venture-backed vet-drug startups pay for screening and deal flow. Sellers (liquidating biotechs, bankruptcy trustees, pharma pruning portfolios) pay success fees.
problem: Roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs exist, and 2026 has brought 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies. Their clinical-stage compounds, with human safety and PK data in hand, are being abandoned because human markets need $300M+ peak sales. Meanwhile animal health has few new molecules for canine lymphoma and osteosarcoma, feline CKD, IBD or chronic pain, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never get IV chemo.
solution: A scouting and licensing studio. It uses AI to mine ClinicalTrials.gov, SEC filings, layoff and bankruptcy trackers for discontinued assets that were not stopped for safety. It scores each for target conservation in dogs and cats, allometric dosing, market size and eligibility for FDA CVM expanded conditional approval. It packages dossiers with a vet development plan and KOL letters, then brokers options, licenses or asset purchases, keeping a finder's fee plus equity or royalty in each spun-out newco.
why_now: The supply of stranded assets is at a peak (layoff tracker, 300 zombies, wobbling software-only AI-drug shops like Schrodinger). Precedents are proven: verdinexor, a human-oncology-origin XPO1 inhibitor, became the first oral canine lymphoma drug, and anti-NGF antibodies moved from human programs into dogs and cats. Pet owners increasingly want oncology and chronic-pain options, while roll-ups (GoodVets, Mars) create channels that can absorb new products.
revenue_model: $15-25k 'Vet Opportunity Screen' reports per target class. $25-100k option fees. Finder's fees of 2-5% of deal value, plus 5-10% equity or royalty in spun-out veterinary newcos.
non_obvious_insight: The human 'failure' threshold is a commercial threshold, not a biology threshold. A $50M-peak product is a rounding error to human pharma but a real business in companion animals, where the target biology is often the same. Zombie boards will sell for pennies, so a tiny studio can option assets that incumbents ignore.
first_30_days: Build a database of about 500 clinical-stage assets terminated since 2019 for non-safety reasons, and shortlist 30 with plausible vet indications. Email 15 liquidating boards and 10 animal-health BD leads. Sell the first two $15-25k target-class screens as paid retainers. Aim for the first option agreement within 4-6 months.

title: Tooling Hostage: Repatriate Molds and Dies
one_liner: Extract molds, dies and fixtures from Asian suppliers, refurbish them, and re-home them with US or nearshore shops.
customer: Consumer-product and industrial OEMs with $10M-$500M revenue and $50k-$2M of tooling sitting at Asian contract manufacturers, plus the new US or Mexican shops that will use it.
problem: Tariffs, a USMCA that was not renewed, and a war shock (freight up to 50%) push companies to move production. The first blocker is the tooling. Ownership is ambiguous, suppliers demand payoffs, drawings are missing, and nobody handles inspection, crating, freight and requalification as one service.
solution: Step 1 is a fixed-fee Tool Audit covering contract review, inspection video, location, condition and cost to escape. Step 2 is turnkey extraction: a local agent and letter, crating, freight and a customs review of the tooling's duty class. Step 3 is US refurbishment and first-article requalification through partner shops. Step 4 is a scan-and-drawing escrow so the next move is easy.
why_now: Companies are re-sourcing now under the rebuilt tariff regime. Freight and war-risk surcharges make each move costly, and the first-mover on tool logistics is unclaimed territory.
revenue_model: Audit at $2.5-5k. Extraction at $8-40k or 10-15% of tooling value. Refurbishment and requalification pass-through at about 15% margin. Escrow subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The lock-in in Asia is the tool, not cheap labor, and the tool's legal owner is often unclear. Whoever holds the tool controls the reshoring decision, so extraction is the real first step. Duty treatment of imported tooling and Chinese export or IP disputes need counsel.
first_30_days: Publish a 'Where are your tools?' checklist. Run 5 audits for hardware brands found via trade shows and Amazon brand lists. Hire a fixer and lawyer in Shenzhen or Ningbo. Line up one refurbishment partner shop in Ohio or Michigan.

title: Pooled Guaranteed Throughput for Agent Builders
one_liner: Mid-market agent builders cannot meet reserved-capacity minimums, so we pool dozens of them into one commitment and sell guaranteed tokens-per-minute with failover.
customer: Agent-heavy SaaS companies and enterprise platform teams with $20k-$300k/month in model spend that hit rate limits and latency spikes at burst but cannot fill provisioned-throughput commitments.
problem: One agent task fans out into dozens of model and tool calls, multiplying request volume 10-50x. Provider tokens-per-minute ceilings and noisy neighbors cause 429s and latency spikes exactly when workflows burst. Reserved throughput exists but is sized for peak and billed monthly, so a mid-market buyer pays for capacity idle most of the day.
solution: A CSP-style aggregator and gateway that buys committed capacity across 2-3 providers, statistically multiplexes customers whose peaks do not coincide, and sells guaranteed-TPM slices with consolidated billing, per-tenant quotas and automatic cross-provider failover. Begin as a failover gateway, then graduate to pooled commitments once demand data proves the multiplexing gain.
why_now: Token prices fell about 67% in a year while agentic usage per task rose 5-30x, so capacity, not unit price, binds at peak. The gateway and sandbox layers are commoditizing (identical sandbox pricing), leaving supply-side pooling as a differentiator.
revenue_model: 10-20% spread on committed spend plus a platform fee for guaranteed-capacity tiers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as price, but for agents the binding constraint is burst capacity when a workflow fans out. Burstiness is diversifiable, like classic insurance pooling, and small buyers cannot pool on their own.
first_30_days: Launch a failover gateway with consolidated billing across Bedrock, Vertex and Azure (no commitment). Sign 10 design partners and collect hourly usage data, model the multiplexing gain, and negotiate the first pooled commitment with letters of intent in hand.
